deficiencies.description: The structured version converts tentative geographic observations into established causal claims. It says gastric and liver cancers in East Asia are "driven by dietary factors and endemic infectious agents" and that migrant studies show the "dominance" of environment over genetics, with Japanese migrants' rates rising "to match the host nation." The lecturer instead posed these as open questions and said the migration result merely "suggests there's something environmental." This overstates causal certainty in a section explicitly intended to teach critical appraisal of epidemiology.

source.evidence: "Why are they high in Asia?"; "we're going to think about different geographic variations of infections"; Japanese migrants "started to develop more breast cancer. So that suggests there's something environmental."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Restore the lecturer's uncertainty: present the patterns and migrant observation as evidence consistent with environmental contributions, not proof of specified causes or environmental dominance.

deficiencies.description: The two-stage model is presented as a universal requirement: "Carcinogenesis requires both initiation ... and promotion." The transcript presents the Berenbaum mouse-skin experiment as evidence for the initiator/promoter concept and says some exposures act as promoters rather than initiators; it does not claim that every cancer necessarily requires both stages. This turns a model/example into an unsupported universal rule.

source.evidence: "This was the first study that really gave rise to this idea. This is the Berenbaum hypothesis"; "Some of them we instead consider to be promoters rather than initiators."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Limit the claim to the experimental two-stage model and to cancers/exposures for which an initiation-plus-promotion framework is being used.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Initiators vs Promoters: The Two-Stage Model, opening sentence

deficiencies.description: The structured epidemiology section removes the lecturer's central cautions about confounding, statistical flexibility, and the limits of association. It consequently does not adequately support the stated learning objective of appraising evidence linking exposures with cancer. The source also uses smoking as strong but not absolute evidence because lung cancer occurs in non-smokers.

source.evidence: "there are lots of cool things you can do with statistics to make your epidemiological study look in whatever way you want. There's lots of caveats. There's lots of confounders"; "you also get lung cancer in non-smokers, so it's not as clear cut."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Retain the methodological caveats and explain that epidemiological associations require careful interpretation rather than simply listing correlations.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Epidemiology and Geographic Variation; Population Epidemiology and Biobanks

deficiencies.description: The pathogen section adds numerous organism-, histology-, and mechanism-specific assertions absent from the source. These include H. pylori causing adenocarcinoma; S. haematobium and squamous-cell carcinoma; HPV oncoproteins disrupting p53 and pRb; and HTLV-1 acting through viral transactivators. The transcript only names H. pylori, schistosomiasis, HPV interference with cell-cycle control "such as p16," and HTLV integration that may affect promoters/expression. These additions are presented as lecture content rather than clearly marked external detail.

source.evidence: "there are also proteins produced by the bacteria that may also play a role"; "helminths, such as schistosomiasis, are at a higher rate of bladder cancer"; HPV proteins interfere with regulatory proteins "such as p16"; HTLV integration "can affect in some way protein expression and cell cycle control."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Remove unsupported specifics or explicitly source them independently; preserve the lecturer's tentative mechanisms where that was the framing.

deficiencies.description: The Burkitt lymphoma mechanism is substantially embellished beyond the transcript: Plasmodium falciparum, class-switch recombination, high-level transcription, the canonical t(8;14), and the claim that MYC is placed under the IGH enhancer are all added. The source supports a malaria/EBV/immunosuppression model culminating in a random heavy-chain-enhancer/MYC translocation, but does not supply these named details. The structured rainfall criterion also changes the source's stated "> 50 mils" to "> 50 mm," an unsupported and potentially material numerical conversion.

source.evidence: "when you look at the malaria map, there is almost a complete identical overlap"; "they're rearranging their heavy chains. They're expressing Myc"; "random chromosomal translocation event where you juxtapose the heavy chain enhancer regions to Myc"; "yearly rainfall of greater than 50 mils."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Keep the mechanism at the level stated in the lecture unless external detail is separately sourced, and reproduce the geographic number faithfully rather than converting it.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Burkitt Lymphoma and the Lymphoma Belt

deficiencies.description: The mutational-signatures section supplies highly specific canonical signatures and lesions not given in the transcript, while omitting the lecturer's main interpretive limitation: real cancer genomes commonly contain mixtures of signatures, so a signature provides an indication of possible exposure rather than proof of a single cause.

source.evidence: "you do see mixtures of lots of different signatures in cancer cells, but it enables us to have some idea."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Add the mixture/attribution caveat and avoid presenting detailed signature mappings not contained in the lecture as though they were transcript-derived.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Methodologies for Determining Carcinogenicity — High-Throughput Mutational Signatures

deficiencies.description: The developmental-susceptibility section adds mechanisms and endpoints not stated by the lecturer: NMU generating O6-methylguanine and fixing mutations in a stem-cell compartment; pubertal mammary ductal branching; atomic-bomb exposure specifically increasing breast-cancer risk; and early pregnancy causing terminal differentiation and reducing progenitor cells. The source gives an association with pubertal female rats, says atomic-bomb-associated cancers were mainly in teenagers/young girls at puberty, and reports the parity comparison without these mechanistic explanations.

source.evidence: NMU "transfers its methyl group, leading to these AT to GC transitions"; "most of the cancers that we saw developed in teenagers ... particularly young girls"; women having children younger "are protected against breast cancer."
source.location: Alkylating agents, atomic-bomb survivors, and parity discussion

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Retain the observations and the lecturer's proposed proliferative-stage explanation, but remove or separately source the additional molecular and epidemiological specifics.

deficiencies.description: The Berenbaum and asbestos subsections add several experimental and cellular details absent from the transcript: permanent versus reversible effects, repeated promotion, papilloma/carcinoma outcomes, macrophage recruitment, and asbestos as a conclusively "pure" promoter. The lecturer used more cautious language—"we think"—and described tumours after initiator then promoter, plus ROS/RNS/cytokines as general features of inflammation.

source.evidence: "when they just put the mutagen, the mice didn't develop skin cancer"; "when they followed it up with ... a promoter, they then did develop tumors"; "we think what happens here"; "We consider this to be promoter activity rather than initiator."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Use the source-level experimental observations and tentative promoter framing; do not add cell-specific or outcome-specific details without an independent source.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Initiators vs Promoters: The Two-Stage Model — The Berenbaum Paradigm and Asbestos as a Pure Promoter

deficiencies.description: Several revision-relevant numbers and examples are lost or weakened: the lecture states that people consume approximately a credit-card's worth of microplastics every day; it gives 70% mouse-rat concordance; and it uses the high-dose saccharin example to explain why dose extrapolation matters. The structured version preserves the latter two ideas but drops the microplastics number and the concrete saccharin example.

source.evidence: "We consume about a credit card's worth of microplastics every day"; "We only see about 70% concordance between mouse and rat"; "we were feeding rats tons and tons of saccharin ... I'd have to be drinking gallons of Coke every day."
source.location: Environmental exposures; animal bioassays and dose discussion

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Restore the omitted numerical/example anchors, particularly where they illustrate exposure magnitude and dose-response interpretation.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Environmental Mutagens; In Vivo Animal Bioassays

deficiencies.description: The structured TCDD account omits the source's associated birth-defects example. This is a distinct toxicological outcome used by the lecturer when describing Agent Orange/TCDD, even though the carcinogenic mechanism is otherwise retained.

source.evidence: "TCDD ... has indirect effects on DNA and is also associated with lots of birth defects."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Retain the associated birth-defects outcome if preserving the full TCDD example.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Chemical Carcinogenesis and Metabolic Activation — TCDD

deficiencies.description: The structured chemical-carcinogenesis sections introduce details not provided in the transcript, including aflatoxin specifically as aflatoxin B1 and on stored grains; cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers; benzo[a]pyrene diol epoxide and an exact G-to-T outcome; TCDD high-affinity/persistent AhR activation; beta-naphthylamine sources and named bladder histologies; and the exact Ames-test organism, minimal-medium protocol, and S9 terminology. Some may be standard background facts, but they have no stated basis in the supplied lecture and are presented as if extracted from it.

source.evidence: The source refers generally to "aflatoxin," thymine dimers, bulky adducts and transversions, "beta-naphthylene," and a histidine-requiring bacterial strain; it does not provide the added names, lesion labels, histologies, or protocol details.
source.location: Aflatoxin, UV, PAH, TCDD, aromatic amine, and Ames-test discussions

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Separate externally supplied technical enrichment from transcript-derived material, or remove it for a faithful structured transcript.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Chemical Carcinogenesis and Metabolic Activation; In Vitro Mutagenicity: The Ames Test

deficiencies.description: The summary changes the lecturer's qualified conclusion—"much cancer is environmental"—into the stronger statement that cancer is driven "heavily" by environmental and lifestyle factors. It also omits the concluding risk-benefit framing: carcinogenic risk must be balanced against benefits (for example, diagnostic X-rays), and exposure dose may be too low to be consequential for many agents.

source.evidence: "much cancer is environmental, including lifestyle-related factors"; "Ultimately, it's all about the risks versus the benefits"; "we're probably not exposed to enough of it in high enough doses to worry about it."

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Use the qualified conclusion and retain dose and benefit-risk context, which are key to applying carcinogenicity evidence responsibly.

source.evidence: Opening identification of the lecturer, six-lecture-course logistics, practical-class references, and "for the NATscis" scheduling comment.

considered.whyNotRaised: These are administrative/course-introduction material rather than substantive revision concepts; their omission or compression is a non-finding under the requested method.

source.evidence: Daily Mail reader comments about smoking, Tai Chi, ginger/garlic, and a cancer-cure conspiracy.
source.location: Bad luck versus environmental exposure discussion

considered.whyNotRaised: These are informal illustrative asides. The substantive points—PAHs in smoke/charred meat, metabolic activation, repair, and dose—are represented elsewhere.

source.evidence: Historical anecdotes about Denis Burkitt treating children with methotrexate in his kitchen and the 1963 formalisation/single-author Lancet publication.
